newsitem.title: USA: MUNI BUYSIDE -- Sit fund moves on less traveled road.
newsitem.headline: MUNI BUYSIDE -- Sit fund moves on less traveled road.

text.p: Michael Brilley, president of Sit Investment Fixed Income Advisors Inc., buys debt other people don't want--but it's far from junk.

In fact, Brilley's penchant for odd ball Baa to triple-A rated bargains including--perish the thought--currently callable issues, has helped land his nearly $300 million Sit Tax-Free Income Fund consistently high on the rankings pile.
For 1996 through September, Morningstar rankings show the fund in the top two percent for total return among funds in its category, according to Morningstar analyst Peter DiTeresa.

Brilley's strategy entails searching the secondary market for issuers like the Reno-Sparks Indian Colony Public Facilities Finance Authority, an Indian tribe that issued bonds backed by revenues from a smoke shop sellng tobacco free of the federal exise tax.
The bonds he likes are complicated, but his strategy is simple.
While the fickleness of interest rates may send other portfolio managers scrambling, Brilley just does what he always does--looks for high-income and low risk.

The Minneapolis-based portfolio manager spurns the plain vanilla general obligation bonds with bullet maturities that many seek because the bonds fail to offer enough yield and are more sensitive to interest rate fluctuations.

Instead, he prefers high-coupon premium bonds with sinking funds that return principal over the life of the bond. The high-coupon provides high income, while the premium coupon and the relatively short average life provide stability. The fund has a six-year average duration, Brilley said.
Sit Fund's preferences when it comes to industry also distinguishes it from from those of other funds, he said.
Housing bonds comprise about 45 percent of the fund, close to five times the weighting the typical fund would give the sector.
Health and hospital issues make up 25 percent, while industrial revenue bonds make up 15 percent of his portfolio.
Within the housing sector, Brilley particularly likes multi-family projects owned by private charities, a relatively new product.

One such issuer bought properties from a private owner who had purchased them from the Resolution Trust Corportation at a bargain cost. The first mortgages on the properties were pooled together to reduce risk.
Because charitable organizations' aims are different, they tend to provide amenities such as low-cost child care and transportation, resulting in longer tenure from residents.
In addition, charities will often provide informal help to residents to keep up with payments.
As for a bond deal's structure, Brilley likes the callable issues many other portfolio managers avoid.
Because relatively few buyers are interested, Brilley gets paid more yield when he buys the bond, which may never end up being called.

One such success story involved some Farmington, New Mexico Pollution Control debt. Though the bonds have been callable since 1988, they haven't been called yet. The insured bonds have a 6.1 percent coupon, he said.
DiTeresa, Morningstar's analyst, said the current market environment showcases Brilley's strategy.

"Right now this year has been a very good demonstration of how well this fund does in a bear market. Most of its peers have been clobbered and it hasn't (been)," DiTeresa said. "They keep their interest rate risk low and that fares very well in years like this year, also it did the fund very well in '94."
Sit's strategy works less well in a bull market because of its affinity for shorter duration bonds, he said.
"When rates are going down, the longer your bonds are the better," DiTeresa said. "This fund keeps on the short side so it doesn't make those big gains."
For instance while the fund make good in an absolute sense in the bull market of 1995, it failed to match the big strides made by longer duration funds, he said.
--Kathie O'Donnell, 212-859-1655
